lesson.grammar_point: present perfect for experience with ever and never, and the past simple for the details

listenings.text: Every semester I invite four or five guest speakers to my marketing course. People often ask me: how do you choose them? It's simple. First, I ask: what have you done? I want people who have worked on real projects, who have launched campaigns and made mistakes. Second, I ask: have you ever taught before? Many of my best guests have never taught. That's fine. I just ask them to prepare a short slide deck, bring one good case study, and leave twenty minutes to take questions. Last year a guest from a startup gave the best class of the semester. She had no teaching experience, but the students loved her stories.

Hi, it's Priya again. Have you ever taught a class? I have, but only three times. The first time was last March, at a university in Pune. It was a workshop about marketing data for thirty students. I was very nervous. I've given many presentations at work, but students are a different audience. They ask a lot of questions! I prepared too many slides, and I didn't finish. But the case study worked very well. The students analyzed the data of a real online store, and they loved it. Since then, I've taught two more workshops. I've never given a full course, but maybe next year.

paras: Many business schools invite professionals from the market to teach. Students like them for a simple reason: they have done the work. A marketing director who has launched real campaigns can explain things that a book cannot. So schools often start with a small invitation: come as a guest speaker for one class.

What do schools look for? Experience is the first thing. A school wants to know what projects you have worked on and which companies you have helped. The second thing is teaching. Have you ever given a lecture? Have you ever run a workshop? Many professionals have never taught before, and that is normal. A school will often give them a short workshop or two guest classes first.

Professionals who teach well usually bring real case studies from their own careers. They prepare a short slide deck, not a long one, and they leave time to take questions. One more thing: they listen to the audience. After a few classes, some of them write their own syllabus and teach a full course. For many, it starts with one invitation, and one yes.
